direct_claims: This chart compares countries' learning-adjusted years of schooling with their Electoral Democracy Index in 2020.
The horizontal axis is the Electoral Democracy Index, described as ranging from 0 to 1, where 1 is most democratic.
The vertical axis is learning-adjusted years of schooling, measured in years.
The subtitle states that learning-adjusted years of schooling combines the quantity and quality of education into one metric.

The source line names World Bank methodology for schooling and V-Dem for democracy, and the Our World in Data branding indicates the chart was presented for public explanation and comparison of cross-country development patterns.
In education research, learning-adjusted years of schooling is meant to reflect not just how long students stay in school, but how much effective learning that schooling produces.
That means two countries with similar years in school can differ on this measure if student learning outcomes differ.
In democracy research, the Electoral Democracy Index is an expert-based measure of how democratic a country's electoral system is.
The chart is cross-sectional for 2020, so it compares countries at one point in time rather than showing change over time.
Because not every point is labeled, the image supports broad comparative interpretation better than exact country-by-country enumeration.
derived_claims: The chart indicates a broad positive relationship: countries with higher electoral democracy scores tend to also have higher learning-adjusted years of schooling. — derived from reading the overall upward association from plotted points.

Countries from Europe and Oceania appear concentrated toward the upper-right portion of the chart, while many African countries appear lower on both measures. — derived from comparing regional clusters by legend category and point positions.

The pattern in the chart suggests that stronger democratic institutions often coexist with stronger educational outcomes, though the relationship is not perfect and there are visible exceptions. — derived from comparing spread and exceptions around the overall positive association.

For example, some places such as Hong Kong and Singapore appear to have very high learning-adjusted schooling despite being well below the highest democracy scores on the x-axis. — derived from reading labeled outliers from point locations.
